## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Karim and Ingrid both want proof of missed bookings on their own lines before paying, so that group fits and is plainly named, while Andreas (who already has his numbers and finds the licence costs more than it recovers) and Hannes (who rejects robot bookings outright) rightly stand apart.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all four speak to price and value.

founder.order_why: Screen 22 ('Offer a pilot?') comes after I had already named my first step as the €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel on screen 20, so the pilot question sits in step 5 when it belongs with the commitment in step 4.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20 and 22: the paid pilot at one location is my commitment step, and screen 22 asks again whether to offer a pilot. Screens 3 and 4 also carry the same kicker and question, so they read as one question shown twice.
founder.missing: No screen let me say that the €3,000 pilot fee is refunded if the hotel is not happy and credited to the licence on roll-out. That is what makes my pilot 'zero risk', and without it strangers see a plain €3,000 up front.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The 'One more thing' screen sits between 5 of 6 and 6 of 6, which breaks the count, and screen 4 quotes a monthly fee of €1,000 to €2,500 that I was never asked about.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 8 both come back to the €3,000 up front, first as what it is worth and then as whether I would pay it, so they overlap a little.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: There was no question on the monthly fee, which screen 4 assumes I gave. Nothing asked how missed calls are covered today (after-hours call center, overflow, voicemail) or what a lost booking is worth per call. Nothing asked about connecting to our CRS/PMS or about handling calls in several languages.

screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel plus the monthly fee yourself, or would the hotel's owner have to agree? I could sign off myself · The hotel's owner would have to agree · Several people would have to agree · It's someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, it makes sense to ask what else stands between wanting Codyco and buying it, and with guest calls that is the data protection check.
screens.why2: A data protection review is exactly what our Datenschutzbeauftragter would run on anything touching guest calls, so I understand it at first reading.
screens.why3: I have taken call-recording and CRS tools through our data protection officer before, so I can estimate this from real experience.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover everything from quick to very long, 'It wouldn't be needed' is a real answer, and 'I can't tell' is the right way out for a purchase I haven't made.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks: it names Codyco, which I was already shown, and 'guest calls' is how I would put it myself.
screens.why6: Heard as four options and then two, it is short and easy to hold, and 'or say you can't tell' comes last as a single escape.
screens.why7: Every option measures how long the review would take; the five bands turn on a 4-week edge with 'It wouldn't be needed' last, there are three answers for and three against, and the review is a real brake on my side for a German hotel group.

screens.why1: Right after I said the data protection review would take 4 weeks to 3 months, asking what eats that time is the obvious next question for me.
screens.why2: The words are plain, but the 4 weeks to 3 months was for the data protection review, and now it is 'buying Codyco', so I have to work out whether they mean the review or the whole purchase.
screens.why3: I know exactly what drags: our data protection officer, the works council on recording guest calls, the DPA with the vendor, and the owner's sign-off.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: Codyco is named as on the idea card, and nothing of the founder's own terms or roles reaches me in words I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: You said the data protection review would take 4 weeks to 3 months. What would take that time?

screens.why1: After the price, who pays, sign-off and the data protection review, asking whether I would actually start with a pilot is the obvious last question of the buying part.
screens.why2: A money-back pilot at one hotel and a demo on sample call data are words I use with vendors every quarter, and €3,000 is a figure I read at once.
screens.why3: I am the one who would approve a pilot for one of our hotels, so I can answer this from how I actually buy.
screens.why4: There is a firm and a soft yes, then a soft and a firm no; they are distinct, and the free demo first is exactly what I would ask a new vendor for.
screens.why5: The pilot, its price, the money back and the one hotel all come through as a clear offer, and no internal term of the founder's reaches me.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one question with four short answers; the first repeats the stem, but three thousand euros says cleanly and I can hold the list.
screens.why7: The first yes is the founder's whole step, and the soft yes is a free smaller step that costs no money, data or signature; the order is firm yes, soft yes, probably not, no, with no escape, so the belief can hold or fail.
